sections.title: Describe the construction and operation of retractable soot blowers.

pages.text:
Unit A-12  •  Elements of Boiler Systems
Objective 2
Describe the construction and operation of retractable soot blowers.
Retractable soot blower systems are used for cleaning solid fuel-fired boilers.
Retractable Soot Blowers
Retractable soot blowers are required in the radiant zone of the boiler. Heat transfer surfaces in
the radiant zone include the furnace waterwalls, radiant superheaters, and reheaters. In these
high temperature zones, the soot blowers retract when not in use. If they remain in place without
steam flowing through them, they overheat, sustain damage, and require replacement.
Short Retractable Wall Blower
A short single-nozzle retractable wall blower removes waterwall ash deposits (Figure 2). With
some fuels, such as coal and municipal waste, ash contained in the fuel may melt in the high
temperature found in the radiant zone of the furnace. Te ash may then come into contact with
the comparatively cool furnace wall tubes. Tis causes the molten ash to solidify on the tube walls.
Additional ash that is created adheres to this original mass. Tis buildup of ash, referred to as slag,
can greatly restrict heat transfer.
Te retractable blower has a short-stroke lance that penetrates the furnace waterwall 25 to 50 mm,
through special openings. Te lance has a jet at its end. Tis jet is angled back slightly toward
the furnace wall, and blasts superheated steam or air against the slag deposits. Te lance rotates
through 360°and cleans approximately a 1.5 m radius.

Long Retractable Soot Blowers
Long retractable soot blowers remove deposits from the convection and radiant heating surfaces,
such as those located in the superheater and reheater banks.
Tese radiant and higher temperature convection zones are cleaned with long, fully retractable
lances (Figure 4). Te lances penetrate the spaces between major heat absorbing sections.
Figure 4 – Long Retractable Soot Blower

Figure 4 shows a photo of an installed soot blower.
Te long retractable soot blower has a drive motor mounted to a carriage. When retracted, the
soot blower remains out of the direct heat of the flue gas. Unlike the wall-mounted soot blower,
this blower hangs from a carriage that is supported outside the boiler furnace.

Unit A-12  •  Elements of Boiler Systems
Te soot blower lance is made of two cylindrical concentric tubes. Te inner tube (the internal
feed tube) remains stationary, and conveys steam from the poppet valve to the outer tube. Te
outer tube (the lance) has a nozzle at the end for blowing steam, and extends into the radiant
zone. A sealing arrangement prevents steam from escaping between the internal feed tube and
the lance. Te lance is motor driven in spiral fashion by an electric motor.
When the soot blower drive is energized, the drive motor rotates a pinion gear which moves along
a toothed rack. As the pinion rotates, it pushes the soot blower lance into the furnace. At the same
time, the drive motor causes the lance to rotate through a chain and sprocket arrangement. Te
lance moves along guide rails located on each side of the beam, into the boiler. Rollers on the
inner support assist in supporting the lance.
A linkage connected to the carriage opens the soot blower poppet valve as the lance begins to
move inward. Tis admits steam to the soot blower feed tube and lance, and begins the cleaning
cycle.
Te carriage advances the lance tube into the boiler until a forward position limit stop is reached.
Te carriage then reverses direction and retracts from the boiler. When the carriage begins to
retract, it slips back a defined amount. Tis causes the lance tube to return on a diﬀerent nozzle
path, and a diﬀerent portion of the tubes are cleaned.
When the lance is nearly fully retracted, it strikes the poppet valve linkage, and closes the valve to
shut steam oﬀ to the soot blower. Once fully retracted, the carriage strikes a limit switch and shuts
down the drive motor. Tis also initiates the next soot blower, if the system is using an automatic
soot blower program.
If a retractable soot blower lance becomes stuck in the boiler furnace, it must be removed manually.
An alarm will activate when this occurs. Steam flow to the soot blower must be maintained until
it is fully retracted, because the steam is necessary to cool the lance. If the steam is shut oﬀ, the
lance will overheat and sag, making it impossible to remove without shutting down the boiler.
Te lance normally has two opposed nozzles at the tip. Te nozzles emit a jet of superheated
steam or compressed air perpendicular to the lance, as illustrated in Figure 5.
While the lance traverses the boiler, it rotates. Tis forms a helical blowing pattern which
eﬀectively cleans the tubes and spaces between tubes in a superheater, reheater, or economizer
bank of tubes.

Unit A-12  •  Elements of Boiler Systems
Objective 3
Describe the construction and operation of stationary soot blowers.
Stationary Soot Blowers
Stationary non-retractable soot blowers are used in lower temperature zones (convection zones),
such as the economizer, generating bank, and air heaters. Tis is because the lower temperatures
in these zones will not damage the soot blower lance.
Stationary soot blowers, like that shown in Figure 7, are used in the convection tube banks and
economizer sections of watertube boilers. Where a number of soot blower units are installed,
their use is normally sequenced, starting at the combustion chamber through to the economizer.
Tis allows the ash and soot to be moved to a specific point in the boiler for removal.
Figure 7 – Stationary Soot Blower
Chain
Steam
supply
Gooseneck
Lance

Boiler Fireside Cleaning Systems  •  Chapter 6
With stationary soot blowers, the lance tube is not retractable; however, it is free to rotate. Te
lance is held in place with bearings. Te bearings are clamped or welded to the watertubes. Te
lance has holes that blast jets of steam between the rows of tubes, keeping the flue gas passages
clear. Te pressure at each steam jet must be strong enough to clean the flue gas passages. Tis
requires a properly sized steam supply, and adequate steam pressure.
Tis type of soot blower can be operated manually with a chain, or with a crank handle at the back
of the blower. It can also be equipped with a motor and operated automatically with a control
system. Figure 7 shows a typical stationary soot blower inserted into a packaged boiler. Note the
chains and reduction gear mechanism used for rotating the lance.
Figure 8 shows the blowing pattern of a multi-nozzle stationary soot blower. It is used where there
is not enough space for the single-nozzle type, and where the flue gas temperature is suﬃciently
low to allow the nozzles or elements to remain permanently in the gases. By rotating, the lance
cleans substantially more area than a non-rotating lance.
Figure 8 – Multi-Nozzle Stationary Soot Blower Pattern

Air Heater Soot Blowers
Air heater soot blowers are of a diﬀerent design and operation. Tey consist of a series of flat
stationary nozzles, situated over the top of the heat exchange surface. Tese nozzles blow
high-pressure steam down onto the surfaces. Ash is blown free, and falls from the tubes into a
dust collection hopper below. Some finer ash particles are carried in the flue gas stream, where
they are separated by using mechanical means, electrostatic precipitators, or both.

Unit A-12  •  Elements of Boiler Systems
Soot Blower Operation
According to ASME BPVC Section VII, during soot blowing periods, the boiler should be
operating at a minimum 50 percent load to ensure stable combustion. Furnace pressure should
be below atmospheric, to prevent blowback through inspection doors and other openings.
On smaller packaged and field-assembled boilers, the operation and sequencing of soot blowers
is done manually. For large boilers with multiple soot blowers, the correct soot blowing sequence
and timing is performed under automatic control.
Figure 9 shows the control screen for soot blower sequencing and operation. Tis screen tells the
operator which blower is in operation, and which blower is next in the sequence. Te operator
can bypass soot blowers that are out of service, or change the soot blower sequence. Operators can
conduct full blows, or partial blows, based on certain operating criteria (such as draf conditions
and temperatures). Te system also alerts the operators of soot blowers that may be stuck inside
the furnace.
Figure 9 – Control Screen for Automatic Soot Blower Operation

A pilot that burns without turndown throughout the entire time a burner is in
service, whether or not the main burner is firing.

A chain grate stoker.

A specialty furnace designed for high intensity heat release from solid fuels,
so named because of its swirling gas and fuel Àows.
Deaerator
A component used for removing oxygen and other corrosive non-
condensable gases that may be dissolved in boiler feed water.
Diaphragm gas valve
A safety shut-oႇ valve for gaseous fuels that uses the diႇerential pressure
across a Àexible diaphragm to drive it open or shut.
Dissolved gases
Gases, such as oxygen and carbon dioxide, which may be in solution in
water.
Dissolved solid
A solid impurity in solution with water. In boilers, calcium and magnesium
salts are scale-forming dissolved solids.
Double block and
bleed
An arrangement of normally closed valves, with a normally open valve
aႈxed to a take-oႇ located between the normally closed valves. It is
designed to ensure a positive interruption of Àuid Àow, especially a fuel.
Draft
A diႇerence in pressure that causes gases to Àow into and out of a furnace.
Excess air
Air in addition to the amount of theoretical air needed for complete
combustion.
External water
treatment
Treatment of boiler feedwater prior to its introduction into the boiler.
Factory-built chimney
A chimney made of various factory-built, interlocking, modular components.

See Àuidized bed combustion (FBC).
FBN
See fuel based nitrogen (FBN).
FD fan
See forced draft fan (FD Fan).
Feedwater
Water introduced into a boiler during operation. It includes make-up and
return condensate.
Firebrick
A common form of refractory made of aluminum silicates, with silica (SiO2)
content varying up to 78%, and alumina (Al2O3) content up to 44%.
Fixed carbon
The solid combustible residue that remains after a fuel particle is heated,
and the volatile matter is expelled.
Flash point
The temperature at which a Àammable liquid produces suႈcient vapour to
momentarily support combustion.
Flue gas
The gaseous products of combustion in the Àue to the stack.
Fluid power gas
valve®
A brand name for a motorized gas safety shut-oႇ valve.
Fluid-Àred burner
A device for mixing liquid, gaseous, or pulverized solid fuel with oxygen, for
the purpose of combustion.

A process where a bed of granulated particles is maintained in a mobile
suspension by an upward Àow of air or gas.

Term
De¿nition
Fluidized bed
combustion (FBC)
A process where a fuel is burned in a bed of granular particles that are
maintained in mobile suspension by the Àow of air and combustion
products.
Fly ash
A product of the combustion of solid fuel. Fly ash is comprised of very fine
particles, which are carried out of the furnace with the Àue gases. Fly ash
ranges in size from about 1 micron to 300 microns.
Foaming
The continuous formation of bubbles with suႈciently high surface tension,
so they remain as bubbles above the disengaging surface. This interferes
with the natural steam disengagement process and can result in priming.
Forced draft
The use of mechanical devices to provide positive gas passage into and out
of a furnace.
Forced draft fan (FD
fan)
A fan that supplies combustion air, under pressure, to fuel burning
equipment.
Freeboard
The space or volume above the upper surface of the bubbling bed, and
below the furnace exit.
Fuel based nitrogen
(FBN)
Nitrogen found within the chemical makeup of a fuel, through ultimate
analysis.
Fuel oil
Homogeneous hydrocarbon mixtures, in liquid form, used in combustion
processes to provide heat.
Galvanized piping
Steel pipe coated with zinc, in order to prevent corrosion.
Guard valve
In a piping system, a valve that is only operated in still liquid, so that it
suႇers little wear and can therefore maintain a tight seal.
Hammer mill
A device used to reduce the size of solid particles, such as coal, by
repeated blows.
Hardness
With regard to water quality, a measure of the amount of calcium and
magnesium salts in boiler water. Usually expressed as grains per gallon or
ppm as CaCO3.
Hard-seated valve
A globe-type valve with seats and plugs made of hard metallic material.
Hartford loop
See return loop.
Herbaceous fuel
Fuels sourced from grasses and straw. These may be in the form of chips,
hog, pellets, or bales.
Hog fuel
A fuel made of coarse wood chips and tree bark.
Hot well
A reservoir at the base of a steam condenser in which condensate
accumulates.
Hydramotor® valve
A brand name for a motorized gas safety shut-oႇ valve.
ID fan
See induced draft fan (ID Fan).
Incomplete
combustion
A combustion process that produces combustible products. These products
can subsequently react with oxygen to produce non-combustible products,
heat, and light.
Induced draft
The use of mechanical devices to withdraw gases from a furnace.
Induced draft fan (ID
fan)
A fan that exhausts hot gases from a furnace, as the combustion products
develop.
Intermittent blowoff
The blowing oႇ of boiler water at intervals.
Intermittent pilot
A pilot that lights automatically each time there is a call for heat, and burns
during the entire period that the main burner is firing.
Internal water
treatment
The softening, deaeration, and conditioning of water inside the boiler shell
or drum, through the addition of chemicals.

Term
De¿nition
Interrupted pilot
A pilot that lights automatically each time there is a call for heat. The pilot
fuel is cut oႇ automatically at the end of the main burner Àame establishing
period.
Ion exchange
A process in which undesirable ions in water are exchanged with more
desirable ions.
Ion exchange water
softener
Equipment used to soften water, using the principles of ion exchange.
LiqueÀed petroleum
gas (LPG)
Petroleum products that consist of light hydrocarbons (butane, propane, or
a mixture of the two) which have been liquefied through the application of
pressure.
Low Àre start
The requirement for a burner to have its fuel and combustion air Àows at
their minimum respective settings prior to ignition. Burners with proven low
fire start use interlock switches to prevent ignition if the fuel and air are not
in low fire position.
Low water fuel cut-off
(LWCO)
A safety device that will shut oႇ a boiler if its water level becomes too low.
Lowest permissible
water level (LPWL)
The lowest water level at which a boiler can be operated without sustaining
damage due to overheating, as determined by the boiler manufacturer.
LPG
See lique¿ed petroleum gas (LPG).
LPWL
See lowest permissible water level (LPWL).
LWCO
See low water fuel cut-off (LWCO).
Make-up water
The water added to a boiler system to compensate for water lost through
exhaust, blowdown, blowoႇ, leakage, and others.
Mass burning
The act of burning municipal solid waste in a single combustion chamber.
Mass burning
facilities
Facilities that burn municipal solid waste in a single combustion chamber.
Mechanical atomizing
oil burner
A burner that uses the pressure of the oil for atomizing.
Mechanical stoker
A device consisting of a mechanically operated fuel feeding mechanism and
a grate. It feeds solid fuel into a furnace, distributes it over a grate, admits
air to the fuel for the purpose of combustion, and provides a means for
removal or discharge of ash.
Mercaptan
A foul-smelling odourant added to natural gas and propane to aid in leak
detection.
Mill
See coal pulverizer.
Modulating pressure
burner
An oil burner of variable firing rate, achieved by varying (modulating) its
nozzle pressure.
MSW
See municipal solid waste (MSW).
Mud
With regard to boiler waterside operations, a combination of suspended
matter and precipitates that settle and accumulate in the lowest-situated
parts of boilers.
Municipal refuse
Untreated solid waste material as collected from household and commercial
establishments. It is highly variable in appearance, density, and BTU
content.
Municipal solid waste
(MSW)
Untreated solid waste material as collected from household and commercial
establishments. It is highly variable in appearance, density, and heat
content.

Term
De¿nition
Natural draft
Where no mechanical means is used to provide air for combustion. AirÀow
into the combustion chamber is the result of warm air being less dense than
cool air.
Natural gas
A homogeneous, combustible mixture of light gaseous hydrocarbons,
primarily methane and ethane.
Natural gas liquids
(NGL)
Hydrocarbon liquids found in natural gas at the wellhead. NGLs include
ethane, propane, butane, isobutene, and pentane.
Net stack
temperature
The diႇerence between the ambient temperature of combustion air, and the
Àue gas temperature at the Àue outlet of an appliance.
NGL
See natural gas liquids (NGL).
NOX
Oxides of nitrogen, including NO, N2O, and NO2.
Odourant
A chemical added to gaseous fuels and liquefied petroleum gases to aid in
leak detection. See Mercaptan.
Outage
The planned or unplanned stoppage of boiler operation.
Overfeed stoker
A stoker in which fuel is fed onto grates above the point of air admission to
the fuel bed.
OverÀre air
In a stoker-fired boiler, combustion air delivered above the burning fuel bed.
Overfire air promotes turbulence and complete combustion.
Peltier cooler
A thermoelectric device that produces a cool surface that condenses any
moisture out of the Àue gas before it reaches the measuring sensor.
PFBC
See pressurized Àuidized bed combustion (PFBC).
PID control
A controller which combines the features of proportional, integral, and
derivative controllers. Commonly referred to as a three-mode controller.
Pilot burner
A small burner used to ignite a large burner.
Precipitation
softening
To soften water through the addition of chemicals that precipitate dissolved
calcium and magnesium compounds.
Premix burner
A burner designed to burn gaseous fuels, where the mixing of fuel and
air occurs within a venturi or mixing tube prior to entering the combustion
chamber.
Pressurized fluidized
bed combustion
(PFBC)
A form of Àuidized bed combustion wherein the furnace pressure is several
times greater than atmospheric pressure.
Primary air
Combustion air that is premixed with fuel before being admitted to a
furnace, or the combustion air admitted below the fuel bed of a stoker-fired
boiler.
Primary air fan
A fan to supply primary air for combustion of fuel.
Priming
With regard to boiler operation, an undesirable condition, in which excess
quantities of water are carried along with the steam to the steam outlet.
Proximate analysis
A measure of the moisture, fixed carbon, volatiles, and ash content of a fuel.

A factory-built chimney, designed to maintain a positive internal pressure
without leaking combustion products through its assembled sections.
Puff back
A minor combustion explosion within a pulverizer system, boiler furnace, or
setting.
Quick-opening valve
A valve that requires a 90 degree turn (or less) of its operating mechanism
to change from fully closed to fully opened.

Untreated water.
RDF
See refuse derived fuel (RDF).

Term
De¿nition
Refractory
Temperature-resistant ceramic material used in boiler furnaces to protect
metal surfaces around burners, line fireboxes, seal openings, or make
baႉes.
Refuse derived fuel
(RDF)
A solid fuel prepared from municipal solid waste. The waste material is
usually refined by shredding, air classification, magnetic separation, or other
means. The fuel may be packed, chopped, pelletized, pulverized, or be
subjected to other mechanical treatment. Further refinement to either a gas
or liquid yields a fuel of the synthetic type.
Refuse derived fuel
facilities
Facilities that use mechanical methods to shred municipal solid waste,
remove its non-combustible components, and burn the remainder to
produce thermally generated power.

A trough or channel in an underfeed stoker, extending within the furnace,
through which fuel is forced upward into the fuel bed.

A condensate return piping arrangement, installed on steam heating boilers.
It prevents low water conditions by stopping the backÀow of boiler water into
condensate return lines.
Returns
Condensate that returns from steam-consuming processes.
Reverse osmosis
A method of reducing the dissolved solids in raw water by passing it through
a semi-permeable membrane.
Ribbon burner
An atmospheric premix burner design that uses rows of serpentine metal
plates as burner head orifices.
Rising stem valve
A gate or globe valve whose handle or stem changes in position when
operated from fully closed to fully open.
Rotary cup oil burner
A burner in which atomization is accomplished by feeding oil to the inside of
a rapidly rotating cup.
Safety shut-off valve
(SSOV)
A fast-closing valve that automatically and completely shuts oႇ the fuel
supply. This is in response to an operating limit or a safety limit.
SAGD
See steam-assisted gravity drainage (SAGD).
Saybolt seconds
universal (SSU)
A measurement of oil viscosity, as determined using a Saybolt Viscosimeter.
Schedule 80
A pipe weight designation that is similar to extra-strong.
Sealing valve
A guard valve.

A valve that seals without forceful contact between a plug or gate and a

Air needed to complete the combustion process, admitted near the

Shock service
Piping or piping system components designed to withstand sudden cyclical
loading due to changes in pressure, temperature, or other mechanical
forces.
Shot
Small diameter steel balls, sometimes used in fireside cleaning systems.
Shrinkage
A sudden reduction in boiler water level as the steam production rate
decreases.
Single-element
feedwater control
A boiler water control strategy that determines the position of the feedwater
control valve only based on drum level.
Slag
In boilers, a mass of fused ash, in its molten or solid state, formed in high
temperature furnace zones.

Term
De¿nition
Slow-opening valve
A valve that requires at least five 360 degree turns of the operating
mechanism to change from fully closed to fully opened.
Sonic cleaning
See acoustic cleaning.
Soot blower
A mechanical device for discharging air, steam, or water to clean the fireside
of boiler heat transfer surfaces.
SpeciÀc conductance
The conductance of a 1 cm3 cube of a solution. Specific conductance is

A metal plate used to atomize the fuel in an atomizer of an oil burner.

See safety shut-off valve (SSOV).

See saybolt seconds universal (SSU).

A continuous pilot.
Steam-assisted
gravity drainage
(SAGD)
The use of high-pressure steam to enhance heavy oil recovery from
underground formations.
Stoker
A device consisting of a mechanically operated fuel feeding mechanism and
a grate; used for the purpose of feeding solid fuel into a furnace, distributing
it over a grate, admitting air to the fuel for the purpose of combustion, and
providing a means for removal or discharge of refuse.
Surface blowoff
The intermittent or continuous removal of water, foam, and impurities from
the water surface of a boiler.
Suspended matter
Solid material entrained in water, such as sand, mud, clay, sewage, and
vegetable matter. Suspended matter may Àoat on the water surface, or it
may be dispersed.
Swell
A sudden increase in boiler water level as the steam production rate
increases.
TDS
See total dissolved solids (TDS).
Tertiary air
Combustion air provided in addition to primary and secondary air; used to

The amount of air required to supply the oxygen theoretically necessary to

combustion (3 Ts)
Time, temperature, and turbulence.
Three-element
feedwater control
A boiler water control strategy that determines the position of the feedwater
control valve by considering drum level, steam Àow, and feedwater Àow.
Total dissolved solids
(TDS)
The concentration of dissolved solids in a sample of a solution, usually
expressed in ppm (parts per million by mass). It is often estimated from
conductivity or sodium concentration measurements.
Tramp metal
Ferrous metal contaminants entrained within a solid fuel.
Travelling grate
stoker
A stoker similar to a chain grate stoker except it has grate elements

For a burner, the ratio of maximum rated firing rate to minimum stable firing

Forms of grates, located adjacent to a retort, through which air is

feedwater control

control valve by considering drum level and steam Àow.

A measure of the elemental composition of a fuel, including the percentages
of carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur, and ash.

A solid fuel firing system that introduces fuel through retorts located below
the point of air admission to the fuel bed.

In a stoker-fired boiler, combustion air delivered below the burning fuel bed.

formation of clinkers.
Urban wood fuels
Wood fuel derived from urban activities. These fuels include packaging
materials, oႇ-cuts from manufacturing, wood remainders from construction
and demolition, yard trimmings, urban tree removal, and from land clearing.
Valve class
A number that represents a combined temperature and pressure service
rating for a valve or piping fitting, in accordance with American National
Standards Institute B16.34 Code.
VCM
See volatile combustible material (VCM).
Vibrating grate stoker
A sloping grate conveyer that delivers solid fuel into the combustion zone of
a boiler by using vertical plates that oscillate back and forth in a rectilinear
direction. This causes the fuel to move into the active combustion zone.
Viscosity
The measure of the internal friction or the resistance to Àow of a liquid
(thickness).
VOC
See volatile organic compounds (VOC).
Volatile combustible
material (VCM)
In a solid fuel, such as wood or coal, the substances that vapourize and
burn during combustion.

compounds (VOC)
Organic chemicals (typically hydrocarbons) with a high vapor pressure (low

A chamber below a stoker grate or surrounding a burner, through which

Damage to the surface of a valve seat, gate, or plug, caused by long-

Chipped woody biomass with a defined particle size, produced mechanically

Wood that has been pulverized and pelletized under heat and high

A type of globe valve with the bonnet and stem at an acute angle with the

Boiler Fireside Cleaning Systems  •  Chapter 6
Objective 4
Describe falling shot cleaning methods.
Falling Shot Cleaning
Falling shot cleaning is a method for removing soot and ash deposits from economizer, tubular
air heater, and superheater tubes. Its use is generally restricted to large watertube boilers with the
superheater, economizer, and air heater zones installed directly above each other. Te system is
fully automatic, and can be continuous or intermittent in operation.
Iron shot or pellets, 6 mm in diameter, fall by gravity onto the surface of the tubes and ricochet
from one tube to another, thereby dislodging deposits. A hopper at the bottom of the boiler
section collects the shot. Te shot is then returned pneumatically to a distributing chamber at the
top of the section for recycling.
Most of the ash removed by the shot is carried away in the flue gas stream. Any large particles fall
with the shot into the collecting hopper. Tese ash particles are recirculated with the shot until
they are broken up into fine particles, and carried away by the flue gas.
Advantages of this method of cleaning the surface of boiler tubes include:
a) A supply of air or steam for the operation of soot blowers is not required. However, air
is required for the pneumatic conveying system to return the shot to the top distributing
chamber.
b) In small plants, the turbine steam supply is not aﬀected by the steam consumption of the
soot blowers.

Unit A-12  •  Elements of Boiler Systems
Chapter Summary
Steam generators, especially those burning solid fuels, create significant amounts of ash. For
example, a single coal-fired unit may produce 15 tonnes of ash per hour. Much ash carries away
with the flue gas stream, and it is removed mechanically or with electrostatic precipitators.
Te remaining ash accumulates on the boiler fireside. Tis ash must be removed from the boiler, or
it will negatively aﬀect boiler eﬃciency and steam production. If its flue passages become plugged
with ash, the accumulation can force a boiler offline. Fireside cleaning is therefore essential to
ensuring unit availability and maximum boiler eﬃciency.
Tis chapter discussed the following fireside cleaning methods:
a) In-Service Methods
i. Soot blowers
•
Retractable
•
Non-Retractable
ii. Sonic Horns
iii. Rapping
iv. Falling Shot
v. Explosions
b) Out-of-Service Methods
i. Hand Lances
ii. Scraping
iii. Sand Blasting
iv. Chemical Cleaning
Power Engineers are responsible for the safe and eﬃcient operation of the plant systems under
their control. Fireside cleaning is an important aspect of this responsibility, regardless of the size
and type plant under their control.

Elements of Boiler Systems  •  Unit A-12
Unit Summary
Tis unit addressed the diﬀerent types of systems designed to ensure successful operation of
boilers. Combustion, fuel, draf, feedwater, blowoﬀ, blowdown, and soot blowing systems are
essential for maintaining eﬃcient and safe heat transfer.
Tis unit emphasized two major operations in a plant’s thermal processes:
1. Te production of heat, through the interaction of diﬀerent fuels, fuel firing systems, and
combustion air systems.
2. Te production of heat transfer fluid (steam or water). Tis included treating makeup
water, recovering condensate, maintaining feedwater flow, controlling the waterside
solids concentration, and maintaining fireside cleanliness.
